sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a text extraction of the Louisiana copy (the extractor did not keep every table column, so placement was checked against the course's own reading of 2026-11-09 in ems-sources.ts). EMR: CPR and AED, tourniquet and wound packing, naloxone, oral airway, BVM, oxygen; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector, aspirin, oral glucose, CPAP, 12-lead acquisition (not interpretation), transport. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways and a limited list of IV and IM medications including dextrose and glucagon. Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, intubation and the wider formulary. No newer model was found 2026-11-11 (EMS.gov's page was unavailable; the only other 'update' found is the 2017 change notice adding tourniquets, wound packing and naloxone to EMR and EMT).

brief.situation: 16:05. You are the AEMT on an ambulance with an EMT partner at a highway crash: a 28-year-old motorcyclist, about 75 kg, came off at highway speed and hit the guardrail. Bystanders took his helmet off. Fire has made the scene safe.
handover: St. Anne's Community Hospital (no trauma surgeon on site) is 8 minutes away; Regional Medical Center, a Level I trauma center, is 22 minutes away.
Within AEMT scope: IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, tourniquets, oxygen, monitoring. No blood products or tranexamic acid on your unit.
Your partner can do one task at a time: hold pressure, take vital signs, or drive.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Scene time and the drive run on the clock; he keeps bleeding inside until a surgeon stops it. Fluids help his pressure but can make the bleeding worse.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends at the hospital, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: About 1.3 L already lost (a quarter of his blood volume) when you reach him. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. A deep forearm laceration with a spurting radial artery bleeding about 120 mL/min. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. A splenic injury bleeding about 25 mL/min at an SBP of 90, faster at higher pressure. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Each 2 L of crystalloid dilutes clotting enough to raise the internal bleeding rate by half. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Half of an infused crystalloid volume stays in the circulation over the minutes of a transport. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A 500 mL bolus through an 18-gauge line with a pressure bag: about 5 minutes.
An 18-gauge IV in a shocked patient: about 2 min (in a moving ambulance too).
A forearm tourniquet: about 20 s.
A cuff cycle: about 45 s.
Scoop stretcher, onto the cot and loaded: about 3 min.
St. Anne's is 8 min away (authored).
The Level I trauma center is 22 min away (authored).

why.question: How much fluid did you give and to what end point, and why that destination?

parts.label: Fluids to a target
parts.criteria: Stop the bleeding you can (the arm tourniquet) first; IV en route rather than delaying on scene; 500 mL boluses, reassessing BP and radial pulse after each, to SBP about 90 or a radial pulse and alert mentation, not to a normal BP; no wide-open running; medical direction after 2 L; keep him warm. Raising the pressure and diluting clotting factors increases internal bleeding.
parts.modelAnswer: Tourniquet on the arm first. IV on the way, then 500 mL boluses, rechecking the blood pressure and radial pulse after each, aiming for a systolic around 90 or a radial pulse and a clear head, not a normal pressure. Never wide open; call medical direction near 2 L; keep him warm. More pressure and more saline make the spleen bleed faster.

parts.label: Destination
parts.criteria: SBP < 90 and HR > SBP are red field-triage criteria (and the tourniquet is one too): the highest-level trauma center, even though it is further; scene time under 10 minutes; trauma alert.
parts.modelAnswer: SBP under 90 with a heart rate above it, and an arm needing a tourniquet, are red criteria: the Level I center, 22 minutes, because he needs a surgeon to stop the bleeding inside. Off the scene within 10 minutes, with a trauma alert.

noProgress.rationale: He arrives alive at a hospital that cannot stop internal bleeding; a transfer to the trauma center follows. This case calls it recovered.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: fluid end point and destination

expertPath.text: Spurting forearm: tourniquet at once. Primary survey: talking, tachypneic, weak fast radial pulse, cool and clammy, tender bruised left upper abdomen: hemorrhagic shock, likely spleen.
Oxygen, monitor, BP 85/53 with HR above it: red criteria. Wet clothing off, blankets. Load for the Level I center.
Wheels rolling; trauma alert. IV en route; 500 mL bolus, recheck: SBP about 90, radial pulse back. Slow to keep-open.
Pressure drifting below 90: another 500 mL, recheck. Call medical direction if approaching 2 L. Never wide open.

arrest.headline: He arrested from blood loss
arrest.body: Two things kill him here: the arm bleed you can stop and the spleen you cannot. Look at the tourniquet time, the scene time, and whether fluid was given at all or so much it drove the bleeding.

traumaCenter.headline: To the surgeons with a pulse
traumaCenter.body: Tourniquet first, a short scene, the right center, and saline in measured boluses to a radial pulse. That is the expert path.

traumaGaps.headline: Right place, harder route
traumaGaps.body: He made it to the trauma center. Check the scene time, the tourniquet, and whether the fluid followed a target or a feeling.

community.headline: The wrong hospital for a bleeding spleen
community.body: SBP below 90 with a heart rate above it and a tourniquet are red field-triage criteria: the highest-level trauma center, even 14 minutes further.

scoring.modelReasoning: Stop the bleeding you can first: a tourniquet above the spurting forearm wound. The bruised, tender left upper abdomen with a fast weak pulse, cool clammy skin and SBP in the 80s is hemorrhagic shock from bleeding you cannot stop, so he needs a surgeon. SBP below 90 with a heart rate above it, and a tourniquet, are red field-triage criteria: the highest-level trauma center, with scene time under 10 minutes and a trauma alert. Start the IV en route. Give 500 mL boluses and reassess after each, targeting SBP about 90 or a radial pulse and alert mentation, not a normal pressure; never run wide open; involve medical direction after 2 L. Prevent hypothermia.

target.ask: While the IV goes in: what is your fluid end point for him?

choices.label: SBP about 90, a radial pulse, alert
Two liters as fast as possible

target.explain: NASEMSO: 500 mL boluses to a target SBP of 90 (a palpable radial pulse or alert mental status), reassessing after each; medical direction after 2 L.
